newsitem.title: BURMA: Burma woos visitors as flak continues from abroad.
newsitem.headline: Burma woos visitors as flak continues from abroad.

text.p: Burma prepared to launch its official tourism year as its military rulers came under renewed attack for their latest crackdown and continued suppression of the democracy movement led by Aung San Suu Kyi.

The government's "Visit Myanmar Year" officially begins on Monday. The State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) hopes the promotion will attract up up to 300,000 visitors over the next 12 months. Myanmar is the military regime's official name for Burma.

"We need to make the world know that Myanmar has a variety of tourist attractions. Only then will people come and visit our country," Hotel and Tourism Minister Lieutenant-General Kyaw Ba said late on Friday.
Lieutenant-General Khin Nyunt, head of military intelligence and Secretary One of the SLORC, recently said Visit Myanmar Year would help negate recent bad reports about Burma.

"Fabrications and biased stories of some foreign news agencies...have made false impressions of Myanmar on those who have not been here," he said. "The main purpose of Visit Myanmar Year 1996 is to enable many tourists to visit Myanamr and see the facts.
"On their return they will explain the true situation they experienced and all the fabrications will be rebutted."
The official start to the tourism year comes amid a new crackdown on democracy supporters.
Last Saturday, the motorcade in which Suu Kyi and other supporters were travelling was attacked by hundreds of stone-throwing, stick-wielding men.
Suu Kyi, the 1991 Nobel Peace laureate and leader of the National League for Democracy (NLD) party, blamed the government for orchestrating the incident.
Western governments and human rights groups condemned the attack and the SLORC's continued refusal to hold talks with the NLD on how to bring democracy back to Burma.
The government denied involvement, and said it was just another move by the democracy movement to dissuade tourists from visiting the country.

Since being released from six years of house arrest in July, 1995, Suu Kyi has urged foreigners not to invest in or visit Burma, saying it would only benefit a handful of people -- mainly connected to the government.
Human rights organisations say the SLORC forcibly displaced people to build hotels or improve infrastructure as part of the preparations for Visit Myanmar Year.
They also said the government used forced labour for infrastructure projects.
The government argues that the tourism year has already benefited many Burmese people and that overall it will help the public more than the government.
Kyaw Ba said that of the $70 million earned by the tourist industry in 1995-96 (April-March), only $4.5 million went to the government.
He said the construction and operation of hotels offered well-paying job opportunities for thousands of skilled and unskilled workers.
Some tourism workers said Suu Kyi's call on foreigners to boycott Visit Myanmar Year could have a negative impact on their business.

"I support the democracy movement and Daw Aung San Suu Kyi," said one tourist guide. "But I don't like her telling people not to come. I have 50 people working for me, and about 500 people are dependent on them. What will they do if people don't come?"
Ironically for the government, one of the country's top tourist sites is Suu Kyi's house.
When the road is not blocked off by the government, as it was on Saturday, tourists pose for photographs in front of her house.
